vignette:
The Weight of What He Saw

Marco is twenty-five years old and works at a car dealership on the outskirts of a mid-sized city in the Netherlands. He is charming by nature - quick with a smile, easy with small talk - and his colleagues consider him one of the better salespeople on the floor. His girlfriend, Lena, has been with him for three years. To most people who know him now, he looks like a young man who has his life reasonably together. What they do not know is that two years ago, Marco spent four months in eastern Ukraine visiting extended family, and that what he witnessed there has not left him for a single day since.

He had gone in the spring, intending to stay for six weeks. His mother's family lived in a small city that had, until then, felt relatively insulated from the worst of the fighting. Within his first month, that changed. Marco was present during a sustained period of shelling that destroyed several buildings on his relatives' street. He helped carry a neighbor - a man he had shared meals with - out of rubble. The man did not survive. Marco watched people he had come to know scatter, grieve, and disappear. He stayed longer than he planned because leaving felt impossible, and then because the routes out became complicated, and then because he was simply frozen. By the time he returned to the Netherlands, something fundamental had shifted in how he experienced the world.

In the months after coming home, Marco tried to resume his life. He went back to work. He and Lena moved into a small apartment. On the surface, he was present. Underneath, he was somewhere else entirely. He finds it almost impossible to explain to Lena what happens when a car backfires in the parking lot, or when a truck rumbles too loudly past the dealership windows. His body responds before his mind can intervene - heart hammering, hands going cold, a sudden and absolute certainty that something terrible is about to happen. He has learned to excuse himself to the bathroom in those moments, to wait it out alone.

Sleep is its own ordeal. Marco rarely makes it through a night without waking, sometimes screaming, sometimes simply sitting bolt upright in the dark with the images already fading but the terror still fully present. He dreams of the rubble, of the neighbor's face, of sounds he cannot unhear. During the day, he moves through long stretches of numbness punctuated by moments of overwhelming distress. He has stopped watching the news entirely. He avoids the Ukrainian community center in his city, even though he once found comfort in that connection. He tells himself it is because he is busy.

At work, Marco's performance has become inconsistent. There are days when he is genuinely excellent - animated, focused, closing deals with the ease that once came naturally to him. There are other days when a customer says something that lands wrong, or when the showroom feels too loud and too bright, and he retreats into a flat, distant version of himself that his manager has noticed and gently mentioned twice now. Marco laughed it off both times.

He has not spoken to anyone professionally about what happened. He told Lena some of it, in fragments, early on. But he saw how frightened it made her, and he decided - quietly, without discussion - that he would manage it himself. He carries a persistent and exhausting sense that he is fundamentally changed, that the person who boarded the plane back to Amsterdam is not the same one who left, and that no one around him quite understands the distance between those two versions of himself. He is not sure he understands it either. He just knows that the world no longer feels safe in the way it once did, and that he is very tired of pretending otherwise.
